scenes.title: Standalone Subnets
scenes.narration: Subnets have appeared in every network lab so far — inline inside the VNet in lab six, generated by for each in the last two. This lesson slows down and writes them by hand, one resource per tier, and shows why the standalone form is the one real networks are built with.

scenes.narration: This is lab twelve. Lab six tucked subnets inside the VNet block. The last two labs generated them from a map. Both work — but both assume subnets are interchangeable. When each tier needs different treatment, its own firewall, its own delegation, you write them out, one resource each. That's today's form.

scenes.heading: Why the standalone form wins
points: Inline subnets live inside the VNet block — compact, but closed
Per-subnet resources (NSG, delegation) need a subnet to reference by id
Standalone subnets are addressable: azurerm_subnet.web.id
The pattern every later networking lab builds on
scenes.narration: Why does the standalone form matter? Because a subnet that is its own resource has an identity — an I D that other resources can reference. An inline subnet belongs to the VNet; there's nothing to point a security group at. The moment a subnet needs to be treated as a thing — firewalled, delegated, peered — it has to stand alone. That's the form this lesson builds, and the form the coming N I C and N S G labs rely on.

scenes.narration: As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. This one is deliberately small — readme, main dot t f, terraform dot t f — because the lesson is about form, not volume.

The setup first, and one absence matters. Locals name the region and the group. The VNet is created with its ten eighty slash sixteen space — but look at what's missing. There is no subnets block inside it. The VNet holds the address space and stops there.

Then the subnets, and each one is a full, standalone resource. The web subnet — group name, VNet name, its own prefix. And the app subnet, the same pattern for the second tier. This is lab six's network, rebuilt in the explicit form. Two blocks instead of one, but every subnet is now independently addressable.

One output closes the file: the web subnet's I D. Hold onto it — it's the handle the next lab's network interface will attach to. A resource with an I D is a resource that can be connected to other resources.

scenes.caption: Standalone subnets — each one addressable
scenes.narration: Drawn out: the VNet carries the address space and no subnets. Each subnet is its own resource referencing the VNet, and the web subnet's I D flows out as the handle for later labs. The explicit form buys addressability.

steps.narration: Here's the network, drawn the standalone way.
The VNet carries the address space — and defines no subnets of its own.
Each subnet is its own resource, referencing the VNet by name.
Standalone means addressable: the web subnet's I D flows out for later labs.
Two blocks instead of one — and every subnet can now grow its own features.

scenes.narration: Apply time, and the plan reads like the diagram: group, VNet, then two subnets, each its own line, each its own resource. The output hands back the web subnet's full Azure resource path. That I D is the entire point of the standalone form — the next lab consumes it.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — reaching back for inline subnets
points: Inline subnets are fine for throwaway demos — but they close the door
A per-subnet NSG or delegation needs a standalone subnet to reference
Migrating inline → standalone later is surgery; start standalone
for_each for many identical tiers; explicit blocks for distinct growing tiers
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: inline subnets are fine for throwaway demos — but they close the door. The inline block welds the subnet to the v net, so there's nothing standalone to build on. Two: a per-subnet n s g or delegation needs a standalone subnet to reference. The day you need a firewall on one tier, the inline block gives you nothing to attach it to. Three: migrating inline to standalone later is surgery — start standalone. Converting after the fact means untangling state that was never separate. Four: for each for many identical tiers; explicit blocks for distinct, growing tiers. Choose by shape — and when in doubt, standalone is the safer default.

scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: azurerm subnet as its own resource — one per tier. Two: the v net block defines no inline subnets. Three: standalone subnets are addressable by i d — the door to n s g s, delegations, and service endpoints. Four: the web subnet i d output is the handle for the next lab's n i c. Five: identical tiers use for each; distinct growing tiers get explicit resources.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
